MASHAM , SAMUEL CUNLIFFE LISTER, 1906), English inventor, born at Calverley Hall, near Bradford on the Ist of January (1774-1853), who successively took the names of Lister and Lister and was the first member  of  parliament   elected for Bradford after the Reform Act of 1832. It was at first proposed that he should take orders, but he preferred a business career and became a clerk at Liverpool In 1838 he and his elder as worsted spinners and manufacturers In new mill   which their fathcr built for them at Manningham, and about five years latcr he turned his attention to the problem Of mechanical   wool-combing, which, in spite   of the efforts of E Cartwright and numerous other inventors; still awaited satisfactory solution. Two years of hard work spent in modifying and improving   existing devices enabled him to produce machine which worked well, and subsequently he consolidated his   position by buying up rival patents; as well as by taking out   additional ones of his owI. His   combing   machines came into such demand that though they were made for only {200 apicce he was able to sell them for {120o, and the saving they cffected in the cost of production not only brought about reduction in the of clothing, but in consequcnce of thc increase in the sales created the necessity for new of wool, and In 1855 he was sent sample of silk  waste (the rcfuse left in reeling silk from the cocoons) and asked whether he could find way of utilizing the fbre it contained. The task occupied his time for many years and brought him to the verge of bankruptcy, but at last he succeeded in perfecting silk-combing appliances   which enabled him to make yarn that in one pound, though produced from raw material 'costing only 6d. or Is pound. Another important and lucrative invention in connexion with silk manufacture was his   velvet loom for piled fabrics; and this, with the silk comb worked at his Manningham mill, yielded him an annual income of {20o,00o for many years. But the business was seriously afected by the prohibitory duties imposed by America, and this was one reason why he was an early and determined critic of the British policy of free imports. In I891 he was made a peer; he took his title from the little Yorkshire town of Masham, close to which is Swinton Park, purchased by him in 1888. In 1886 an Albert medal was awarded him for his inventions; which were mostly related to the textile industries, 'though he occasionally diverged to other subjects, such as an air-brake for railways. MASHONA , Bantu-ncgro people, inhabitants of Mashonaland, Southern Rhodesia. The name Mashona has been derivec the contemptuous term Amashuina applied by the Matabele to the aborigines owing to the habit of the latter of rcfuge in the rocky hills with which the country abounds. Before the Matabele invasion about 1840 most of Southern Rhodesia was occupied by the Makalanga, the Makorikori and thc Banyai, all closely related. Most of them becamc subject to the Matabele, but   although they sufered   severely from their attacks, the Mashona   preserved certain national   unity. In 1890 the Mashona came under British protection (see RHODESIA) . The ancient Greek and Roman masks worn by their actors hollow figures of heads had the double object of identifying the performers with the characters assumed, and of increasing the power of the voice by means of metallic mouthpieces. They were derived like the drama from the rural religious festivities, the wearing of mock faces or beards being a primitive custom connected no doubt with many early types of folk-lore   and religion. The usc of the dramatic mask was   evolved in the later theatre through the mimes and the Italian popular comedy into   pantomime; and the   masquerade   similarly came from Italy, Venice. The domino   (originally   apparently an ecclesiastical   garment) was a loose cloak with small half-mask worn at masquerades and costume-balls by persons not  otherwise   dressed in character; and the word is applied also to the person wearing it.

MASK (Fr. masque, apparently from med. Lat. mascus, masca, spectre, through Ital,   maschera; Span. mnascara), covering for the face, taking various forms, used cither as a protective screen or as disguise. In the latter sense masks are mostly associated with the artificial faces by actors in dramatic representations, terror in savage rites) . The spelling masque, representing the same word used morc specially for certain varieties of drama in which masks were originally worn  (see DRAMA) also masquerade; particularly in the sense of a masked ball Or an entertainment where the personages are disguised. Both mask and masquerade " have naturally passed into figurative and technical meanings, the former especially   for various senses of face and head (head of grotesque faces in sculpture), or as equivalent to cloak " QI screen " (as in fortification or other military uses, fencing, &c.) And in the case of death-masks the term is employed for the portrait casts, generally of plaster or metallic foil, taken from the face of dead person (also similarly from the   living) , an ancient practice of considerable interest in art.
